title: Out in haste (Exodus 12:29–42)
hookLine: no time for the bread to rise; they leave that night

cards: A hurried leaving has a look to it. The phone charger still in the wall. The coffee warm on the counter.
The half-packed bag. You take what's in your hands and you go. At midnight in Egypt, the last plague falls.
In the King James Bible: "there was a great cry in Egypt; for there was not a house where there was not one dead." Pharaoh's own son among them.
And in the middle of the night, the king who said no again and again sends for Moses and Aaron.

teach.h: RISE UP, AND GET YOU FORTH.
teach.b: Pharaoh says: "Rise up, and get you forth from among my people." Go. Take your flocks.
Take everything. And then, from Pharaoh himself: and bless me also. The Egyptians urge them to hurry, and there's no time to finish anything.
Exodus records the detail people still taste every year: "the people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneadingtroughs being bound up in their clothes upon their shoulders."

So they bake it flat on the road, unleavened cakes, because they were thrust out and could not wait. That flat bread, matzah, is what Jews eat at Passover to this day: the taste of leaving before you were ready.
Two more details are easy to miss.
First: "a mixed multitude went up also with them." Not only Israelites, and the text doesn't say who they were.
Second, the text stops and counts: four hundred and thirty years in Egypt, and on the very day they ended, the people went out.

teach.h: A NIGHT TO BE MUCH OBSERVED.
teach.b: Then it says the night itself belongs to God: "It is a night to be much observed unto the LORD." A night God kept watch over, so Israel keeps watch on it every year. Christians carry the bread forward too.
Latin-rite Catholics and some Protestant churches use unleavened bread or wafers at communion, recalling the Passover setting of the Last Supper.
Orthodox churches use leavened bread, which Orthodox writers explain as a sign of the risen life. Same table, different loaves.

how: Jews eat matzah through the week of Passover to remember the hurried departure; Latin-rite Catholics and some Protestant churches use unleavened bread or wafers at communion, while Orthodox churches use leavened bread.

practice: Think of the list running in your head right now, emails, laundry, the call, and pick one thing on it that doesn't need finishing today. Picture setting it down like dough that didn't get to rise: not failing, just leaving.
If you pray, you can hand the list to God for a while; if you don't, simply put it down.
